\chapter{Day}
\label{ch:te-day}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} in Telugu and choose between the everyday Persian loan and its formal Sanskrit alternate.}

Say \te{రోజు}, a genuine Persian loan from rōz, and set it against the formal \te{దినము} — the mirror image of Kannada's plain dina.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\te{రోజు}]{\te{రోజు} (rōju) — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} a genuine Persian surprise}

\label{lesson:TE-C23-roju}



\begin{quote}
You might expect Telugu's word for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} to be Sanskrit, like Kannada's \emph{dina}, or native Dravidian. It's neither — it's Persian.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\te{రోజు}} (\textbf{rōju}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{day}\textquotedblright{} — is Telugu's everyday, ordinary word for \textquotedblleft{}a day.\textquotedblright{} Here's the real surprise: it's \textbf{borrowed from Classical Persian} \textbf{\ar{روز}} (\emph{rōz}) — the same root, ultimately, as the Persian day names hiding in words like \textquotedblleft{}Nowruz\textquotedblright{} (\textquotedblleft{}new day\textquotedblright{}). Persian \emph{rōz} itself traces to a Proto-Indo-European root, \emph{\textbf{*lewk-}} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{bright}\textquotedblright{}) — a \textbf{completely different} PIE root from the \emph{\textbf{*dyew-}} family behind Latin's \emph{diēs}, Hindi's \emph{din}, and Kannada's \emph{dina}. Both roots independently mean something like \textquotedblleft{}shining, bright\textquotedblright{} — but they are \textbf{not} cousins; this is convergent meaning, not shared ancestry.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Telugu also has \textbf{\te{దినము}} (\textbf{dinamu}) — the same Sanskrit \textbf{tatsama} word as Kannada's \emph{dina}. But here's the honest twist: unlike Kannada, where \emph{dina} is the plain, everyday word, Telugu's \textbf{\te{దినము}} is the more \textbf{formal, literary} alternate — \emph{rōju} does the everyday work instead. Telugu's formal/everyday split runs the \textbf{opposite direction} from Kannada's.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rōju\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} a genuine Persian loanword
  \item the honest surprise — from Persian rōz, PIE \emph{lewk-, NOT the same root as diēs/din/dina}
  \item the reversed pattern — dinamu is Telugu's FORMAL word, unlike Kannada's plain dina
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What language does Telugu's everyday \textbf{\te{రోజు}} (\emph{rōju}) come from? (\textbf{Persian} — \emph{rōz}.) Is Persian \emph{rōz}'s PIE root the same as Latin \emph{diēs}/Hindi \emph{din}/Kannada \emph{dina}'s root? (\textbf{No} — a completely different PIE root, \emph{*lewk-}, \textquotedblleft{}bright,\textquotedblright{} vs. \emph{*dyew-} — related in meaning, not in ancestry.) Is Telugu's Sanskrit word, \emph{\te{దినము}} (\emph{dinamu}), the everyday word or the formal one? (\textbf{The formal one} — the opposite of Kannada, where \emph{dina} is plain and everyday.)
\end{tcolorbox}
